stories.title: Spirit Airlines Dania Beach HQ Sells at Auction for $93.25M
stories.excerpt: Spirit Airlines’ shuttered headquarters building in Dania Beach was acquired at auction for $93.25 million. A Hill City Capital affiliate was the buyer of the office campus, totaling over 600,000 square feet. The facility was delivered just two years ago. The campus covered more than 11 acres and comprised four buildings, including corporate offices, an amenity building, a crew-training facility with flight simulators and corporate housing. The low-cost carrier shut down abruptly on May 2 after a last-minute bailout from the federal government failed to materialize. About 17,000 employees lost their jobs. With the airline no longer operating, its bankruptcy estate began monetizing its remaining assets. That includes aircraft, equipment, airport-related assets and real estate. Hill City Capital is a Boston-based investment firm and hedge fund founded in 2020. It manages roughly $4.9 billion in discretionary assets focusing on concentrated, long-biased equity strategies within sectors like industrials, transportation, and business services The post Spirit Airlines Dania Beach HQ Sells at Auction for $93.25M appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Spirit Airlines HQ, Dania Beach, sold for $93.25M to Hill City Capital affiliate
600K SF campus with crew training, flight simulators, corporate housing delivered 2 years prior
Airline bankruptcy liquidation; South Florida office market faces distressed inventory pressure
stories.summary: Hill City Capital acquired Spirit Airlines' shuttered headquarters campus in Dania Beach for $93.25 million at auction. The 11-acre, 600K SF facility comprised four buildings including corporate offices, amenity space, flight simulators, and crew training facilities, delivered just two years before the airline's May 2024 collapse. The bankruptcy estate is monetizing real estate and equipment as part of the liquidation process.
stories.impact: Distressed office conversion opportunity in South Florida. The liquidation of a brand-new, purpose-built corporate campus signals weakness in Dania Beach/Fort Lauderdale office fundamentals and may flood local market with conversion or redevelopment inventory, potentially suppressing nearby office valuations and creating tactical land/adaptive reuse opportunities for multifamily developers in the submarket.

stories.title: Payments Manager Corpay Cross-Border Relocates to 18K SF at 560 Lexington Avenue
stories.excerpt: An international payment and currency risk management firm is planning a headquarters relocation to Rudin’s 560 Lexington Avenue. Corpay Cross-Border Solutions, which operates under corporate payments company Corpay, has signed an 11-year lease for 17,778 square feet at the Plaza District tower, Commercial Observer has learned. The landlord declined to provide the asking rent, but an April lease inside Rudin’s 22-story tower asked $84 per square foot, according to previous CO reports. Jacob Rosenthal and Kevin Carroll of CBRE represented Corpay, while Rudin was represented in-house by Kevin Daly and a CBRE team of Peter Turchin, Brett Shannon, Eric Deutsch and Lauren Levy. Corpay Cross-Border plans to move from Tishman Speyer‘s 300 Park Avenue into its new, prebuilt office, which occupies the entire 17th floor of 560 Lexington, this fall. Daly, Rudin’s vice president of office leasing, stated that the deal validates recent portfolio investments, which allowed for minimal modifications to meet Corpay’s space requirements. “This allowed us to accommodate their accelerated timeline for move-in, which was a big factor in getting the deal done,” Daly said. Located two blocks from Grand Central Terminal, the 380,000-square-foot office building at the corner of Lexington Avenue and East 50th Street has seen over 91,000 square feet of leasing activity in the last six months, according to Rudin. Recent arrivals include financial firm Marex, hedge fund SummitTX and coworking firm Industrious. Spokespeople for CBRE and Corpay Cross-Border did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Emily Davis can be reached at edavis@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Corpay Cross-Border, international payments firm, relocates HQ to Rudin's 560 Lexington Avenue
11-year lease, 17.8K SF at ~$84/SF ($1.494M annual); move from 300 Park Avenue fall 2025
Manhattan Plaza District office demand from TAMI/fintech; Rudin recent build-to-suit capital deployed
stories.summary: Corpay Cross-Border Solutions, a payments and currency risk management firm, signed an 11-year, 17,778 SF lease at Rudin's 560 Lexington Avenue in Manhattan's Plaza District at approximately $84/SF. The company is relocating from Tishman Speyer's 300 Park Avenue to an entirely pre-built 17th floor, moving in fall 2025. The deal reflects Rudin's recent portfolio investments enabling rapid tenant accommodation and validates demand for Class-A office space among fintech/TAMI firms.
stories.impact: Modest positive signal for Manhattan office market in TAMI segment, but minimal direct multifamily impact. The relocation underscores that Manhattan office demand remains concentrated in high-spec fintech and financial services; broader office headwinds persist, which may temper net in-migration and job growth that would otherwise support multifamily demand in outer boroughs and nearby metros.

stories.title: Charlotte Apartments Trade for $76.3M
stories.excerpt: Tishman Speyer made its first foray into the Charlotte market, purchasing Berkshire Dilworth, a 296-unit luxury multifamily property between West Midtown and the historic Dilworth neighborhood. Berkshire Residential was the seller of the asset, which traded for $76.3 million, or just over $250,000 a unit. Berkshire Dilworth, located at 1351 E. Morehead St., is 97 percent occupied. The unit mix includes studios and one- to three-bedroom floorplans with an average size of 856 square feet. Interior amenities at Berkshire Dilworth comprise a 24-hour fitness center, a yoga studio, a resident lounge, coworking spaces, a clubhouse and a rooftop lounge with a fireplace. Outdoor offerings include a swimming pool, a sundeck and a terrace lounge. The community also includes 3,000 square feet of street-level retail. Tishman Speyer is planning to upgrade the property’s amenities and exterior, along with select apartment improvements. Newmark’s John Heimburger, Dean Smith and Sean Wood represented Berkshire Residential. The post Charlotte Apartments Trade for $76.3M appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Tishman Speyer acquires Berkshire Dilworth, Charlotte, 296 units at $258K/unit ($76.3M total)
Luxury asset, 97% occupied, West Midtown/Dilworth neighborhood; includes 3K SF retail
Tishman's first Charlotte entry; signals institutional capital pursuing Sunbelt multifamily growth market
stories.summary: Tishman Speyer purchased Berkshire Dilworth, a 296-unit luxury multifamily property in Charlotte's West Midtown/Dilworth neighborhood, for $76.3 million ($258K/unit) from Berkshire Residential. The property is 97% occupied with studios and 1-3 BR units averaging 856 SF, and includes amenities, rooftop lounge, and 3K SF street-level retail. Tishman plans selective upgrades to amenities and select units.
stories.impact: Entry by tier-one institutional developer signals confidence in Charlotte multifamily fundamentals and rent growth trajectory. Acquisition price at $258K/unit in a Sunbelt luxury submarket validates underwriting assumptions for new development in Charlotte; de facto market comp supports elevated development feasibility and attracts additional capital to the market, shortening pre-development timelines for pipeline projects.

stories.title: Investor Team Pays $91.8M for 2 Charlotte Office Buildings
stories.excerpt: Corebridge Real Estate Investors and Crestlight Capital acquired two buildings in The Station at LoSo mixed-use project in Charlotte. Commercial Search reports that the group paid $91.8 million for the assets, which consist of 200,000 square feet of space. Beacon Partners was the seller. At the time of sale, the buildings were 90 percent leased. JLL’s Ryan Clutter, Mike McDonald, Daniel Flynn and Director CJ Liuzzo led the Capital Markets’ Investment Sales and Advisory team that worked on behalf of Beacon Partners. Located at 3600 and 3700 South Blvd., Station 3 and Station 4 represent the first phase of a roughly 15-acre, master-planned development. Slated to come online in three phases, Beacon Partners’ project also includes MAA LoSo and Ello House, two communities totaling 693 units. Future phases will bring online Station 1 and 2, two additional office buildings set to total roughly 1 million square feet, as well as a 350-unit community expected to break ground this year. The post Investor Team Pays $91.8M for 2 Charlotte Office Buildings appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Corebridge Real Estate & Crestlight Capital acquire 2 office buildings, Station at LoSo Charlotte, $91.8M
200K SF office space, 90% leased; part of 15-acre mixed-use master plan with 693 multifamily units delivered
Future phases include 350-unit multifamily community and ~1M SF additional office (Stations 1 & 2)
stories.summary: Corebridge Real Estate Investors and Crestlight Capital acquired two office buildings (Station 3 and Station 4) at The Station at LoSo mixed-use development in Charlotte for $91.8 million. The 200K SF portfolio was 90% leased at sale. The mixed-use project already includes 693 multifamily units (MAA LoSo, Ello House) and plans to deliver two additional office buildings totaling ~1M SF and a 350-unit apartment community in future phases.
stories.impact: Mixed-use placemaking with significant multifamily component anchored by institutional office. The office acquisition validates master-plan economics and suggests capital redeployment within phases; future 350-unit delivery compounds demand pressure on Charlotte market and indicates developer confidence in residential absorption. Institutional capital stacking office+residential signals submarket maturation and may attract additional development to LoSo and nearby Charlotte South Boulevard corridor.

stories.title: NRP Advancing 312-Unit Port St. Lucie Apartment Venture
stories.excerpt: The NRP Group broke ground on its newest luxury apartment community, a 312-unit development within the 10,000-acre Tradition master-planned community at 13661 SW Village Parkway in Port St. Lucie. M&T Bank provided construction financing. Group 4 Architecture designed the project. This marks The NRP Group’s second development closing in Florida this year. Situated on approximately 18 acres, the development consists of 10, 3-story buildings offering a mix of one-, two- and three-bedroom apartment homes ranging from approximately 720 to 1,300 square feet. Every residence will include either a private balcony or a fenced ground-floor yard. Amenities include a 24-hour fitness center with both strength and cardio equipment, a swimming pool, coworking suites and dedicated work-from-home offices, a multipurpose resident lounge with a full kitchen, package concierge and storage facilities, outdoor grilling areas, as well as landscaped courtyards and gathering spaces. Completion is scheduled for summer 2028. The post NRP Advancing 312-Unit Port St. Lucie Apartment Venture appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: NRP Group breaks ground, 312-unit luxury development, Tradition master-planned community, Port St. Lucie
M&T Bank construction financing; 18 acres, 10 three-story buildings, 720-1.3K SF units
Second Florida development closing for NRP in 2025; work-from-home amenities, high-end finishes
stories.summary: The NRP Group broke ground on a 312-unit luxury apartment community at Tradition, a 10K-acre master-planned community in Port St. Lucie, with M&T Bank providing construction financing. The development spans 18 acres across 10 three-story buildings offering 1-3 BR units (720-1.3K SF) with private balconies or fenced ground-floor yards. Amenities include fitness, pool, coworking, multipurpose lounge, and landscaped courtyards.
stories.impact: NRP's second Florida close in 2025 reflects sustained multifamily capital confidence in Florida pipeline despite rate headwinds. Port St. Lucie development within established master-plan signals developer focus on high-amenity, work-from-home-enabled product in secondary Sunbelt markets; successful absorption here may trigger additional development site acquisitions across Florida's mid-tier metros and reinforce institutional appetite for Tradition and similar large-scale planned communities.

stories.title: John McCullough of Kennedy Wilson Multifamily Development: 5 Questions
stories.excerpt: Since joining Kennedy Wilson following the firm’s $347 million acquisition of Toll Brothers’ apartment living platform in 2025, John McCullough has been serving as president of the real estate investment company’s multifamily development group, where he oversees every aspect of the firm’s U.S. development business. Kennedy Wilson’s acquisition of Toll Brothers’ platform gave it general partner interests in 18 apartment and student housing properties, with assets under management of $2.2 billion. The firm also purchased a pipeline of 29 development sites in various stages of construction. Toll Brothers’ entire apartment living management team has transitioned over to Kennedy Wilson under the leadership of McCullough, who previously led apartment living operations at Toll Brothers. But McCullough’s real estate path wasn’t always laid out for him, as he started out in the U.S. Navy and then eventually hit his business stride at school in Boston. Commercial Observer caught up with McCullough last month to discuss his entry into real estate, the Toll Brothers acquisition, and his mission at Kennedy Wilson. This conversation has been edited for length and clarity. Commercial Observer: How’d you get started in real estate? John McCullough: I got started in real estate in a roundabout way. I went to the United States Naval Academy for my undergrad, and graduated in 1994, and then served five years in what we would refer to as the surface navy. If I had stayed in the Navy long-term, I would have trained to be the captain of a ship. I served on two large aircraft carriers out in San Diego, and it was a great experience. It was a really good grounding in the fundamentals of leadership I was put into a lot of situations that were incredibly difficult as a 23- or 24-year-old, but I learned a lot from that. bullets: Kennedy Wilson acquires Toll Brothers' apartment platform, $347M; 29-site development pipeline

Major platform consolidation; Toll Brothers exit signals strategic shift in apartment portfolio
stories.summary: Kennedy Wilson acquired Toll Brothers' entire apartment living platform for $347 million, gaining general partner interests in 18 apartment and student housing properties worth $2.2B AUM and a development pipeline of 29 sites in various construction stages. Toll Brothers' apartment management team, led by former platform head John McCullough, transitioned to Kennedy Wilson. McCullough now serves as president of Kennedy Wilson's multifamily development group.
stories.impact: Significant institutional capital reallocation and platform consolidation. Toll Brothers' apartment exit signals potential strategic refocus toward single-family homebuilding; Kennedy Wilson's acquisition of 29 pipeline sites and experienced management team suggests capital deployment across multiple markets and de facto confirmation of development feasibility assumptions embedded in Toll's original site assembly, likely accelerating delivery timelines and competitive density in those markets.

stories.title: Southern Land Company Hires Tony Marchbanks as Head of Homebuilding
stories.excerpt: Southern Land Company has made a leadership hire to spearhead single-family home development in three key states, Commercial Observer has learned. Tony Marchbanks has joined the firm as national president of homebuilding, in which he will focus not only on the U.S., but also focus particularly on Tennessee, Texas and Colorado, according to Southern Land. Marchbanks brings with him 30 years of real estate experience and most recently served as chief operating officer for Highland Homes, where he launched a building spree in the Houston market, producing 1,000 homes per year, Southern Land said. “Higher interest rates and lack of job growth all culminate into a lack of consumer confidence, so you have all three key contributors to a good homebuilding environment that are headwinds at this time,” Marchbanks told CO. “But for a company like Southern Land, it’s actually a huge opportunity because they have expansion plans, particularly into Texas, which is the largest new home market in the country,” Marchbanks said. “Most builders secured their lot supply three years ago, and now they have too many lots. So it’s an opportunity for a company like Southern Land to find and [invest] in communities they wouldn’t have been able to in a strong market.” Southern Land is currently developing four master-planned communities across 5,000 individual lots in its portfolio. Marchbanks will oversee the construction, purchasing, sales and architecture for those soon-to-be neighborhoods. Southern Land has been making some changes in recent months by launching its own mortgage lending division in May to augment its sales division and support its construction pipeline, CO reported at the time. Build-to-sell homes are not the only residential asset class Southern Land has been dabbling in either, as it builds multifamily properties in Las Vegas; Erie, Colo.; and just outside Austin, Tex. Mark Hallum can be reached at mhallum@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Southern Land Company hires Tony Marchbanks as national president of homebuilding
30-year veteran from Highland Homes (Houston 1K homes/year production); focus Tennessee, Texas, Colorado
Higher rates, lot oversupply from 3-year-old acquisitions create consolidation opportunity for efficient builders
stories.summary: Southern Land Company hired Tony Marchbanks as national president of homebuilding to lead single-family development in Tennessee, Texas, and Colorado. Marchbanks previously served as COO for Highland Homes, where he oversaw Houston production of 1,000 homes per year. He noted that higher interest rates and weak job growth have constrained the homebuilding environment, but created opportunity for well-capitalized firms like Southern Land to acquire overextended lot supplies from competitors who secured land three years ago.
stories.impact: Lateral signal for multifamily: homebuilder lot consolidation and reduced single-family production (due to rates and consumer confidence erosion) may redirect buyer demand toward rental housing, particularly in Texas and Tennessee. Reduced single-family supply and slower delivery timelines in these high-growth metros support sustained multifamily rent growth and development feasibility; multifamily developers should model increased absorption velocity and consider accelerating starts in markets where single-family production is contracting.

stories.title: How Trent Johnson, Brian Landrum at Harbert Management Corp. Invest in Senior Housing

The group has been investing in the seniors housing space for 15 years, raising a $210 million investment fund in 2016 and a $510 million investment fund for the space in 2020. The group is currently on its third fundraise, as they attempt to capitalize on the first wave of Baby Boomers turning 80-years-old in 2016. The duo sat down with Commercial Observer to discuss their careers, how the asset class has evolved, the present and future of the senior housing space, and where the best investment opportunities will be in an increasingly important asset class. Trent Johnson: I started investing in the space in 2012, which is where I met Brian at Fortress Investment Group. I actually came from a legal background. I started out as a real estate lawyer, and then I spent a lot of years at an apartment investment and management company, which was a large multifamily REIT based out of Denver, Colo, Apartment Investment and Management Company. bullets: Harbert Management senior housing team manages $8B AUM, raised $510M fund in 2020
15-year track record in seniors housing; third fundraise underway capitalizing on Baby Boomer aging wave
Baby Boomers turning 80+ in 2016 catalyst; institutional capital pursuing seniors housing asset class
stories.summary: Trent Johnson and Brian Landrum, co-heads of seniors housing at Harbert Management Corporation ($8B alternatives asset manager), have invested in seniors housing for 15 years, raising a $210M fund in 2016 and a $510M fund in 2020. The team is currently executing a third fundraise to capitalize on the first wave of Baby Boomers reaching age 80. The duo discussed how the asset class has evolved and where best-in-class opportunities exist.
stories.impact: Minimal direct multifamily impact; seniors housing is distinct asset class with different underwriting, financing, and regulatory requirements. However, large institutional capital commitment to seniors housing signals demographic demand tailwinds (aging population, lifecycling) that may compress available institutional capital for mainstream multifamily development and increase competition for REIT/fund capital, potentially raising cost of debt and equity for conventional apartment projects in key markets.

stories.title: Sunday Summary: The Rent is Too Damn Low!
stories.excerpt: Back in 2010, Jimmy McMillan ran for governor of New York on a pretty straightforward platform: The rent was too damn high. McMillan said it again and again, and named his political party The Rent is Too Damn High Party. (McMillan’s presence on the debate stage garnered national attention and Matthew Yglesias even titled a slim book with the same name.) Sixteen years later, McMillan is still not wrong, in that the average monthly rent just hit $6,655 in Manhattan according to research from Corcoran Sunshine — which is 10 percent higher than it was a year ago. There are a number of solutions that the Mamdani administration have proffered, but one that has perhaps attracted the most attention has been freezing rents on rent-stabilized apartments. In June, the Rent Guidelines Board issued a freeze on one- and two-year leases, which will certainly be popular with rent-stabilized voters. But one has to wonder if it will actually address the larger issue of affordability — especially if landlords begin to lose more money than they make on stabilized units. Some landlords are keeping units off the market rather than getting them in rentable shape. “Some of [the rent-stabilized units] require more work than others, but for the ones that need significant work — and I mean baseline, just to get them up to livable standards — we’re talking $30,000 minimum,” said Jose Tur, who owns two stabilized buildings in Washington Heights and testified before the RGB before their vote. In addition to the baseline, Tur told Commercial Observer that he would probably have to include another $30,000 per unit for the cosmetic fixes. And that’s on the lower end of the renovation spectrum. Matthew Engel, president of Langsam Property Services, says he has units that require $80,000 to $100,000 worth of work, and rent as low as $600 per month. “There’s no way for me to finance that work,” said Engel. “No bank would lend me $100,000 if I’m only going to be able to collect $6,000 a year in rent.”
bullets: Manhattan average rent $6.655/month, up 10% YoY; rent-stabilized freeze issued June 2025
Rent Guidelines Board froze 1- and 2-year lease renewals; political response to affordability crisis
Risk: rent-stabilized inventory retention if landlord economics deteriorate further
stories.summary: Manhattan's average monthly rent reached $6,655, a 10% year-over-year increase, according to Corcoran Sunshine research. In response to affordability pressure, New York's Rent Guidelines Board issued a freeze on one- and two-year lease renewals for rent-stabilized apartments. However, the freeze may not address underlying affordability and risks landlord underinvestment if economics on stabilized units deteriorate further, potentially pulling rental inventory off-market.
stories.impact: Regulatory risk to New York multifamily development pipeline. Rent stabilization freeze suppresses operator economics on legacy stock and may deter new institutional investment in unregulated (market-rate) inventory if perception grows that political intervention will broaden. Developers should model higher cost-of-capital in NYC and premium pricing for new construction to offset regulatory tail risk; Manhattan market tightness may accelerate outer-borough and nearby suburban multifamily development as capital seeks regulatory clarity and yield certainty.

stories.title: AI-Native Hanover Park Leases Full Floor at 387 Park Ave. South
stories.excerpt: A new lease with AI-native fund administrator Hanover Park and the expansion and extension of PMG Worldwide’s existing space have been recent highlights at TF Cornerstone’s 387 Park Ave. South, which has seen more than 100,000 square feet of leasing activity in the past year. The recent transactions follow K Health’s long-term renewal and the expansion of another TAMI user completed in late 2025. Hanover Park signed a lease for the building’s entire 10th floor, totaling approximately 19,269 square feet. PMG Worldwide renewed its lease on the entire second floor while expanding into the entire third floor, bringing its total footprint to approximately 38,744 square feet. “We’re pleased to welcome Hanover Park to 387 Park Avenue South and to expand our relationship with PMG Worldwide,” said Joe Lanzilotta, Director, Commercial Asset Management at TF Cornerstone. “The property continues to outperform the market as a destination for growing businesses.” The post AI-Native Hanover Park Leases Full Floor at 387 Park Ave. South appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Hanover Park (AI-native fund administrator) leases entire 10th floor, 19.3K SF, 387 Park Ave South
PMG Worldwide expands/renews 38.7K SF (floors 2-3); 100K+ SF leasing activity past year
Manhattan office leasing momentum in TAMI/AI-native segment; TF Cornerstone build-to-suit deployment
stories.summary: Hanover Park, an AI-native fund administrator, leased the entire 10th floor (19,269 SF) at TF Cornerstone's 387 Park Avenue South in Manhattan. Concurrently, PMG Worldwide renewed and expanded across floors 2-3, totaling 38,744 SF. The property has recorded over 100K SF of leasing activity over the past year, including renewals from K Health and other TAMI tenants, validating TF Cornerstone's capital deployment.
stories.impact: Positive office leasing signal in Manhattan TAMI/AI segment but immaterial to multifamily. Concentrated office demand in fintech/AI segments does not broadly support Manhattan office or housing demand; sustained Manhattan office weakness in non-TAMI segments and overall employment uncertainty continue to dampen net in-migration and renter demand. Multifamily developers should remain cautious on Manhattan ramp-up; office strength in narrow vertical does not validate broad-based office recovery.
